assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities and the New Keynesian framework underpin the modern theory and practice of monetary policy. Calvo's price-setting model, Taylor's staggered contracts and policy rule, and Woodford's synthesis of microfounded models with policy design are all widely used, including in central banks. The influence is broad, durable and policy-relevant.
assessment.attribution: Credit is spread across many people (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets, Gertler). Calvo (pricing), Taylor (contracts and rule) and Woodford (framework) are the clearest foundational trio. Gali and the DSGE estimation group (Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets) are reasonable alternatives, and the three-name limit forces hard exclusions.
assessment.maturity: The core contributions date from the 1980s to early 2000s. They have been tested through several decades of monetary policy and through the post-2008 and post-2020 inflation episodes. Recognition is mature.
uncertainties: Where to draw the line between the Calvo/Taylor/Woodford core and the DSGE-estimation contributions of Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets.
The 2021-23 inflation episode has raised questions about the framework, which may affect the committee's reading of its empirical record.
Earlier prizes (Phelps, Lucas, Sargent-Sims, Kydland-Prescott, Bernanke) partly overlap in subject matter.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: This work built the modern political economics of constitutions, electoral rules, state capacity and fiscal policy. It combines formal models with empirical tests across countries. It shaped a major research field and the study of how institutions affect economic outcomes.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the clearest credited pair, through their joint models, books and empirical work on electoral rules and constitutions. Besley's work on state capacity, accountability and taxation is closely related and arguably co-foundational. The trio is coherent, though individual contributions differ in emphasis.
assessment.maturity: The core work dates from the 1990s and 2000s and is extensively cited and replicated. Its core ideas have long been standard in the field.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity; the committee may judge it complementary or too close in subject.
Some causal claims about electoral rules and constitutions have been debated.

I have a disclosed field proximity: Persson co-authored with me on corruption as a collective-action problem, and my own field is political science. I have tried to apply the same criteria as for other candidates, and conflicts are disclosed but not adjudicated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The structural estimation of demand and dynamic industry models (BLP and its extensions) changed empirical industrial organisation and is used in merger analysis, antitrust, trade and regulation. It supplied a standard tool for estimating differentiated-product demand with endogenous prices. The impact is large and applied.
assessment.attribution: Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes (BLP 1995) are the clearest core. Pakes also has a distinct dynamic-games contribution (Ericson-Pakes, and with Bresnahan, Benkard and others). Bresnahan and Reiss have strong claims on the earlier empirical IO tradition, so the boundary of credit is uncertain.
assessment.maturity: The work is thirty years old and routine in academic and policy practice, so recognition is mature.
uncertainties: How the committee weighs BLP against Bresnahan and Reiss's earlier empirical IO work.
Whether the subject is seen as a methods contribution or as a substantive economic discovery.
Some criticism of identification assumptions and of numerical sensitivity in BLP estimation.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Law and finance made the legal and institutional origins of financial development an empirical research programme. It had large effects on corporate governance, development and finance. The impact is very broad across fields.
assessment.attribution: Shleifer, La Porta and Lopez-de-Silanes are the central trio in the legal-origins and investor-protection papers. Vishny's credit rests mainly on the earlier corporate-finance work with Shleifer, so he is a distinct contribution from this specific discovery.
assessment.maturity: The key papers date from 1997 to 2008 and have been heavily cited. Their findings have also been heavily contested, so the verdict is not yet settled.
uncertainties: Replication and measurement concerns about legal-origin indices, and critiques of the causal reading of legal origin.
Shleifer's wider body of work (corporate governance, behavioural finance) may be treated as a separate or larger case.
Non-scientific controversies attached to individual candidates may affect committee judgment.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection in trade, centred on Melitz (2003), changed international trade theory and empirics. The model explains exporter selection, productivity effects and a new channel for gains from trade. It shaped a large body of work across trade, macro and IO.
assessment.attribution: Melitz is the clear originator of the canonical model. Helpman's contributions to firm-level trade (with Melitz and Yeaple, and in related work) are substantial, and Redding's extensions and quantitative work are also credited. Prior prizes (Krugman 2008) cover the new trade theory background, so credit has to be separated from that.
assessment.maturity: About two decades have passed since the main paper, with extensive empirical testing and applications. Recognition is reasonably mature.
uncertainties: How much of the field's credit goes to Melitz alone versus the wider group of authors, such as Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are not in this credited list.
Overlap with Krugman's 2008 prize.
The 1-3 laureate limit may split credit unevenly.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Kiyotaki-Moore model of collateral constraints and credit cycles explains how small shocks are amplified and persist through asset prices and borrowing limits. It became central to macro-finance and informed analysis of the 2008 crisis and later work on financial frictions.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) are the clear originators of the collateral-constraint amplification mechanism. Gertler and Gilchrist belong to the related financial-accelerator tradition, in which Bernanke's earlier Nobel recognition (2022) is a competing credit point. Credit here is clearer for the first pair.
assessment.maturity: The core paper dates from 1997 and the framework has been used and extended for decades, with strong empirical use after 2008.
uncertainties: The 2022 prize to Bernanke, Diamond and Dybvig partly covers financial crises and financial frictions, so the committee may see overlap.
Boundary between Kiyotaki-Moore and Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist credit.
Empirical identification of collateral channels is still debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Task-based analysis of technology and the study of trade shocks transformed the understanding of labour demand, wage inequality and local labour market adjustment. The China-shock work had wide public and academic impact and showed persistent local effects of trade exposure.
assessment.attribution: Autor is the common thread across the task approach, polarisation and the trade-shock work. Katz's earlier work on skill demand and returns to education (with Goldin, who received the 2023 prize for other contributions) and Hanson's work on trade and local labour markets are separate but related strands. Dorn is also credited. The theoretical task framework is also associated with Acemoglu, who is outside this candidate's credited names and already a laureate (2024).
assessment.maturity: The work dates from about 2003 to 2016 and has been widely replicated and extended. Some conclusions are still under revision, so maturity is moderate-to-high.
uncertainties: How credit divides between the empirical strands and Acemoglu's task-based theory.
Debate about the size and persistence of trade-shock effects and about measurement of polarisation.
Possible overlap with the 2019 and 2021 empirical labour-market prizes in method and style.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The long-run top-income and wealth data series created a new empirical base for inequality research and public debate. Their use of tax records changed how inequality is measured, and the work strongly influenced policy discussion and later research.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez (2003) are the clear originators of the top-incomes series. Zucman's work on offshore wealth and distributional national accounts is related and substantial but more recent. Piketty's later theoretical claims (r>g) are more contested than the data contribution.
assessment.maturity: The main data work is more than twenty years old, with strong reception. Parts of the later theoretical and wealth-measurement claims are still being debated.
uncertainties: Contested measurement choices in top-income and wealth estimates, and disputes over the interpretation of r>g.
Whether the committee values data construction and measurement as a Nobel-level discovery, and how it weighs it against analytical contributions.
Saez also appears in the optimal-taxation candidate, which complicates credit.
